strengths: Slide 1 opens with a memorable, brief-specific problem rather than a generic biography: the seminar rule, two definitions of freedom, and paper-cut figures establish the lesson's conceptual and visual premise.

Slides 3–6 turn abstractions into useful relationships: internal pressure, unequal participation, cancel/preserve/transform, and one-sided versus reciprocal recognition are shown as processes rather than bullet summaries.
Slide 4 clearly labels the participation pattern as illustrative rather than measured data, while slide 7 explicitly rejects automatic progress. These are strong integrity safeguards.
Slides 2 and 8 provide effective lesson pacing: a four-part route at the start and retrieval questions with three compact checkpoints at the end.

issues.evidence: The canceled state shows A plus only B, C, and D, while the preserved and transformed states contain A–F. E and F disappear without explanation, contradicting the nearby claim to carry every participant through.
issues.fix: Show all six participants in every state, or explicitly mark E and F as omitted for a stated reason. This is a content/selection defect in an otherwise continuous diagram.

issues.evidence: The institution text extends below the bottom of its beige card; the final line, “time.”, sits outside the container. It is readable but visibly breaks the three-card system.
issues.fix: Increase the card height, shorten the copy, or reduce internal line spacing. This is a generation/layout defect rather than a content problem.

issues.evidence: The source line is substantially smaller and lighter than the lesson content and is unlikely to remain comfortable on projection; similarly small citations recur on slides 3, 6, and 7.
issues.fix: Raise citation size and contrast while keeping it visually subordinate.

A.signatureMoment: Slide 4: the A–F participation model makes the internal contradiction between equal permission and unequal practical participation immediately visible, then previews the structural revision.

strengths: Slide 1 is calm and inviting, with the empty chair circle supporting the seminar premise rather than functioning as unrelated stock decoration.
The typography, margins, and restrained palette remain consistently readable across all eight slides, with no visible clipping or missing assets.
Slide 5 gives Aufhebung a clear three-part verbal decomposition and visually distinguishes cancellation with a strikethrough.
Slide 8 ends with useful retrieval prompts and the memorable reusable lens, “What fails? What survives? What becomes possible?”

issues.evidence: Logic, nature, and spirit appear as three parallel text columns, but the slide does not visually explain how they form the claimed larger system or how the lesson path relates to them.
issues.fix: Show the system and the selected lesson route as an explicit nested or directional map rather than a three-column glossary.

issues.evidence: The three question-mark icons and text columns list prompts but do not demonstrate a position being tested “from within.” There is no visible claim, consequence, pressure, or revision.
issues.fix: Work the seminar example through a connected claim → consequence → internal tension → richer account diagram.

issues.evidence: The three cards name permission, domination, and reciprocity, but no participants, airtime, turns, or directional relationships are depicted. The red label “ONE VOICE · ENTERS AGAIN” is also awkward and does not clarify domination.
issues.fix: Use persistent participant tokens or an airtime sequence so the shift from formal permission to domination and then reciprocal participation can be seen.

issues.evidence: The two outlined boxes state “B can only approve” and “B may answer,” but they do not show the asymmetric and reciprocal relations the lesson is explaining. The slide remains a prose comparison rather than explanatory information design.
issues.fix: Add directional claim, answer, challenge, and blocked-response paths between A and B.

issues.evidence: Individual agency, shared norms, and institutions are again presented as adjacent columns with no connectors. The lower enabled-agency box and caveat are useful, but their relationship to the three levels must be inferred.
issues.fix: Connect the three levels bidirectionally and attach the enabled-agency and revision caveats to the relevant links.

B.signatureMoment: Slide 8: the final reusable-lens panel is the deck's strongest combination of concise language, hierarchy, and lesson utility.

result.reason: Both decks pass the hard checks: eight slides are acceptable because no count or palette was specified; both are English lesson-format decks, contain the required Hegel subject, show no missing images or clipped essential text, and clearly flag the seminar example as illustrative rather than empirical. The preference remains A in either presentation order. I would give A to the user because its additional complexity earns its place: the paper constructions create a distinctive conceptual world, while slides 3–6 use diagrams to reveal pressure, preservation, reciprocity, and institutional mediation. It exceeds competent default quality, although the missing E–F tokens on slide 5 and the card overrun on slide 7 prevent flawless execution. The single most valuable change for B would be to replace the static text-card sequence on slides 3–7 with one persistent A–F participant model that visibly evolves through dialectic, sublation, recognition, and institutional freedom.
result.whatWouldMakeWinnerExceptional: Carry the same six participant tokens without omissions from slides 4 through 7, showing how turn structure becomes reciprocal recognition and then a revisable institution, while repairing the slide 7 card fit. That would turn several excellent individual diagrams into one uninterrupted visual argument.
